utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I see the witness is there. This is not a protected witness, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, no, there are no protective measures in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand it is Mr. Mehmed Ahmic. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, would you please give the Tribunal your date of birth and your place of birth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 6th of January, 1955, in Ahmici Municipality of the Vitez. Currently I'm an unemployed official of the Vitez Municipality, president of the SDA party in Vitez, married, the father of two, and a graduate of the school of management.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please tell us what were your professional activities?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Before the war I was a private entrepreneur and I was active in politics. During the war, for a time, I belonged to the army, and later I worked for the UNHCR. I'm still active in politics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, we would like to discuss the period before the war during which you worked in Ahmici. Can you please tell us on what date and what year you settled in Ahmici, and what exactly were your profession occupations in Ahmici before the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't move to Ahmici, I was born there. My parents live there. I was just away during my education, but for a time I lived in Vitez where I had a Cafe. Just before the war I had a house in Ahmici, which I built in 1989, 1990, and there was a grocery store in it. At the beginning of the multi-party system in the former Yugoslavia, I joined actively in the work of the Party of Democratic Action. In that period, that is from '91 until roughly 1996/'97, I was Deputy President of the party at the municipal level, and for a time I was acting president of the SDA party in our municipality. My house was in Ahmici next to the road, 20 or 30 metres away, that is where I had my shop, that was my source of income, and I participated in politics on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic you recently discussed or mentioned your activities within the political party, the SDA. Could you please also relate to us what this political commitment involved, and also explain to us what type of ideologies you embraced in this particular political commitment.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The very name of the party speaks for itself, a party of democratic action. After the single-party system that we had in the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, a multi-party system was established, and this party rallied the majority of the Bosniak people. I considered it to be democratic, and I've held its principles. That party continues to advocate a democratic, integral free -- united, free and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those were the ideals that prompted me, and that I continue to uphold, even though now I am a member of a different party, it is called the Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, but ideas remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And what date exactly did you begin your activities in the SDA which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't join it. Actually, I was one of the founders of the party sometime in April 1991. I don't remember exactly the date, but that was the time when the party was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What responsibilities, Mr. Ahmic, did you have within this party?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the top leadership at the municipal level. I was the deputy president. If the president was absent, I took over. My main task was to establish a multi-party government in Vitez, because in addition to the SDA there was the HDZ party, the SDS, the Social Democrat the Social Democratic Party, and after the multi-party elections the HDZ was the winner, SDS came second, and SDS, as compared to the population share had only a few seats, but our main task was to establish the executive, legislative and other branches of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you stated that in Ahmici you had a store, or a shop before the war. Can you please describe for us what type of shop this was? What were you selling in that shop?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was privately owned, or as we called it, an independent shop. Its name was Ajla Adi, a combination of the names of my son and daughter, and I sold food stuffs, clothing and even some appliances, but I must point out that previously it was owned by the Vjetrenica socially owned company and I took it over because I worked in that company. But it is important to note that this was a store which both Muslims, Croats, Serbs and passers-by would come and shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You just stated that your clientele was of all communities in Ahmici and in the area, Muslims and Croats. I would like to ask the Registrar -- I would like to ask for the Court deputy, rather, to come forward and show these images to the witness. These are aerial photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, please look at this photograph, it represents a part of Ahmici, the lower part of Ahmici, which is close to the road which goes to Busovaca to Vitez. When we met before this hearing you asked if I would indicate for you where your house is located. You also indicated and we have made a circle around that particular image, there is a circle there, and that is numbered 3. That is indeed the location of your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then, therefore, it is located immediately adjacent to the main road, the southern road?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you please state for us and state for this Tribunal who your neighbours were? Who lived in the houses around your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Next to me were my relatives and neighbours belonging to a different ethnic group, Croats. My late uncle Sakib was to my right, left to my house was a house that was still under construction. Those were just the foundations of a house of the late Pianic. Across the road from me was the house of Ivo Papic. To the right of him the house of Pero and Maria Papic. To the left of Ivo Papic's house is the house of Suad Causevic, Suada and Ahmir Causevic. The next house on the same side as my house is the house of Mesur Ahmic and Mehmed. Then a new house owned by a person from Zenica. Then there was the mosque and the school. This is Ahmir Pezer's house, Nedjo, Kupreskic Vlatko, Zoran and so on. To the right was the house of my mother and my brother, and my two nephews. That is the immediate neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Among the names that you've just stated for us, are most of them Muslim names? Are these Muslim family names among which perhaps you've also indicated some Croatian names? Could you please list them for us, the names of the Croat families that lived near you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The closest house, Croat house, was the house of Ivo Papic, then that of Marija and Pero Papic, then Slavko and Rafael Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, would you please take the pointer and indicate for us on this photograph, on this aerial photograph, the house which you mentioned, that belonging to Ivo Papic, which you said belonged to Mr. Ivo Papic. I see that that house then is across from your house, almost directly across from your house, on the other side of that road. Who lived in that house at the time that you yourself were living in your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th of October, 1992, Ivo Papic, his wife Dragica Papic, his sons Drago and Goran Papic, and daughter. I forget her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before the war, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: And Ivo Papic's daughter-in-law, Dragan Papic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, before the war what relations did you have with the Papic family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Before the war our relations were just fine. Mr. Ivo Papic was a plumber. He was my next door neighbour, a very hard-working man. More than 90 per cent of the houses had water installed by him and the plumbing done by him. So really, we never called anyone else to do any plumbing except him. He did the plumbing for my own house, with another man from Vitez, a Muslim. We were so close that we would say to each other, we would greet each other in the customary way, using the Catholic expression when we talked to them and they would address us with the Muslim expression. We were so close that he was the only one who let me collect to his electricity supply when I was building my new house. Also, with my video camera and my son, I videoed the wedding of his son, Dragan Papic, in the church in Busovaca. It was a church wedding. I think that we still have that videotape. So that is an illustration of the kind of relations we had before October 1992. This also applies to relations with the other Papic, not just me, but the whole neighbourhood. Let me tell you a detail that there were more cases of litigation among Muslims of Ahmici than there were any court cases between representatives of the two ethnic groups, so that relations between the Muslims and the Croats were extremely good. My uncle had an especially close relationship with Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, please direct the bench directly and do not turn towards me.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before October 1992, the events that we will discuss in a moment, you never truly felt that the relations -- the friend relations that you had with your neighbours, your Croat neighbours, were transforming or deteriorating before October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps a little earlier than that maybe in May or June, there was a minor disagreement. I don't want to call it a conflict. Ivo Papic and myself and Moharem (Phoen) Causevic, we were sitting together and talking, and then he said -- he reproached me for hanging up the Yugoslav flag for the official holiday. On the one side of the shop I had the Yugoslav flag and the other the SDA flag. And my explanation was that this was the official flag of the country which had still not been declared null and void, and this was a public facility, and that I felt it my duty to do that. So that was the first time we had a sort of argument, with a drink. And I think that what bothered him most was the SDA flag rather than the official Yugoslavia Slav flag. However, the first check board flag that was hoisted was on the house of Ivo Papic. Of course, I have nothing against it as a symbol of a nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, we will come back to the events of October 1992 and also the circumstances in which you had to leave your home and leave the Ahmici village. Would you please relate to this Tribunal what happened at that time, and in what circumstances you had to leave Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I left Ahmici under very difficult conditions. In fact, I only just managed to escape alive. On the 20th of October, 1992, I think it was about 7.30 in the morning, actually, before that, maybe about 5.30, I was woken up by a strong explosion. I was sleeping in my bedroom with my wife and small children. The explosion was a direct hit into the minaret of the mosque because I can see the minaret from my bedroom window.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I'm sorry, let me interrupt you. I think it's preferable for clarity that you discuss what happened the day before, before the 20th of October, because I believe that before that there were a number of events which will enable us to understand more clearly what happened thereafter. So, please, I think it's best that you begin at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th of October in the evening, a checkpoint or a barricade was put up in front of my house, and this was done because, according to some assessments and intelligence reports, the HVO army was allegedly to go towards Jajce, but, in fact, it was going to Novi Travnik where there was already a conflict underway between the army and the HVO. A checkpoint was placed to prevent it. I came there. I called up a certain number of people. I asked whether this checkpoint should be put here or somewhere else. They said that was all right, but I insisted that it shouldn't be right in front of my house, but that it should be moved a little. So it was moved towards the cemetery, in a bend there in the road. That evening, there was guard duty. The checkpoint was operational, so it was not possible to pass through it, and I think the persons manning it would check passengers, their documents, and would not let them pass, so that transport was suspended. In line with my political duties, I visited the checkpoint and went to sleep about 1.00 in the morning. That was what preceded the 20th. I went to sleep, tension was high, and in the morning I was awakened by the explosion that I already mentioned when the minaret of the mosque was hit. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. I would like for you to specify a number of things. This roadblock that was on the road near the Catholic cemetery, was this erected by the Muslim residents of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What exactly was the purpose of this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The precise objective was to control the passage of civilians and armed people on the road between Busovaca and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: These people coming from Busovaca and going in the direction of Novi Travnik, were these Croats?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were units of the Croatian Defence Council. In fact, I think they were special units because Jajce was just about to fall to the Serb aggressors, and allegedly they were going to assist there. But according to intelligence reports received by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as there was a conflict ongoing in Novi Travnik, that, in fact, they were heading towards Novi Travnik to help the HVO in Novi Travnik. So I think that one of the reasons for this roadblock was to prevent these forces from going to Novi Travnik, and they were, in fact, prevented. They didn't pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You stated that on several occasions during that day, on the 19th of October, you went to that roadblock. How many Muslim persons from Ahmici were manning this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Twenty on the outside, but this figure changed. There were seven or eight, at other times, 10 or 15, because this went on all day and all night. Some people would go and others would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did these persons have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You, yourself, during that day of the 19th of October, were you carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you please give us an account of that day, of the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: As I had started telling you, a strong explosion woke me up, the shell that had hit the minaret of the mosque, about 5.30 in the morning. As we couldn't sleep anymore, we got up. My wife, at about 7.30, wanted to open the shutters. I think you understand what I mean. They are wooden shutters that we have on the windows because the windows were French windows from the living room, and she opened the shutters. The moment she did that, from Dragan's house, there was a burst of fire that hit her. The children were already alive. We all fell to the ground. We managed to crawl into the corridor, and then the shooting started. I managed to hide the children beneath the staircase, and my mother-in-law, who was with me at the time, because she was sick, she had cancer of the breast and she had been operated on, I managed to evacuate them to the business premises beneath the staircase. After that first burst of fire, only then did I realise what was happening, because fire started from all sides. About midday, artillery started shelling from Hrasno and the house had already started burning. I crawled back to the first floor and to the loft to try and save some of our clothing and some of our technical appliances. I was in contact all the time with, let me call them, the joint bodies of government in Vitez for as long as the telephone lines were operational. I was in contact with Mr. Sefkija Dzidic, Ivica Santic, Fuad Kaknjo. These were the people who were the military and civilian leaders in Vitez. A lot of people called me because there was a conflict going on, the house was burning, and they wanted to see whether I was alive, because the house had been set on fire with inflammable bullets from the roof. I insisted on fire brigades coming to extinguish the fire. I called by phone. However, towards the afternoon when the line had already burned, Ivica Santic, who was with Fuad Kakanj, told me to save my life and to try and save my wife and children because, I'm quoting him, "Both armies were out of control, and if I didn't help myself, there was no one that could help me." I realised that there was no help coming from anywhere. The fire was coming from three sides, this side, this side, and this side. My only possibility was to flee this way, and there was an Opel Record parked here. When there was a lull, about 4.00 in the afternoon, we were in the house all that time, we went through the door, my wife, my daughter, my wife's sister, and my mother-in-law, and they ran to Sakib Ahmic's house, my uncle's house. I followed them, crawling. While they ran across, there was no fire. I think they could have killed them, but they didn't. When I came out, then again fire was opened at me, but I crawled behind the car. I was carrying my small son, who was three and a half or four, under my arm, and I could hear voices from the woods saying, "Surrender," that they would call the fire brigades and that they would extinguish the fire. Then an anti-aircraft gun started shooting. I could see, as I crawled as I left the house, and I saw Dragan Papic manning the anti-aircraft gun. I went zig-zag. I crawled zig-zag so they wouldn't hit me. The holes left by the shells from the gun were like this, not to mention how many bullets whizzed past my head. I don't know how I survived. I reached my uncle's house. I managed to crawl again to Omer Pezer's house here, and then slowly I reached Bekbir (Phoen) Ahmic's house, and then behind the mosque I reached the upper mosque. I think -- no, I don't think, I know for sure, that the fire was coming from the direction of the wood just below Dragan Papic's house, as far as I was able to see. I could see from my house, because my house was on a high level, Dragan Papic, Fahir (Phoen) Milicevic, Pero Papic, and some other soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, we are now going to go back over some of what you stated for some clarification. You stated that you woke up on the 20th of October, you were awakened, rather, by relatively heavy armed fire which was targeting the minaret, the minaret of the mosque, the lower mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also stated that your house was also the target of this firing; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You also stated, and please try to tell us, if you can, where this fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The fire was coming from infantry weapons from the woods just behind Ivo Papic's house, and the area of Hrasno where the artillery was. It is an elevation which is about two kilometres away from my house as the crow flies. And several months earlier, these pieces had been positioned there, two anti-aircraft guns, about two months before. I'm not a soldier but I think that the ammunition is about 40 millimetre calibre. My house was a direct target. It was the only house to be set on fire during that so-called first conflict between the army and the HVO. And I think all the other houses remained intact, except for a couple of sheds and a couple of stables.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, your house was the object of fire of the type of weapon you described, the anti-aircraft gun, which was located at a somewhat relatively long distance from your own home. Were other shots also directed at your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Infantry weapons, anti-aircraft guns, and automatic rifles. I said that the first burst of fire came from the house of Ivo Papic and Dragan Papic. I think it was he because he had sand going up to the window, and I saw this when we opened the shutters, both me and my wife, and we were extremely surprised. Behind the house too, there were infantry weapons, an anti-aircraft gun. From the area of Zume, therefore, from the area of the cemetery, from these three sides, the fire was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So your house was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me clarify something before we move on. The witness said there was a first burst of fire from the house of Ivo Papic and Dragan Papic. "I think it was he because I saw this when we opened the shutters," it should read. Who is the "he" that is referred to? Perhaps the witness could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Papic. I could see it when I opened the shutters. That is when the fire started. As soon as we opened the shutters, they realised we were in the house, that we were alive, and they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: May we please show Exhibit 30 to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, what does this photograph represent?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: This is Dragan Papic's house and Ivo Papic's house, the father and the son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, where was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from the direction of my house, approximately, or maybe from the main road which divides my house from Ivo's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So the side that we see now is the side which faces the road and also next to your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, my house too, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th of October, did the firing come from that house, and could you please specify if that is the case?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, from this window (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You are now showing us a window on the right side of that building on the upper level. Who was located at that window?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Dragan Papic in a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon? Did he have a weapon in his hand?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he make use of this automatic weapon, of this automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first round of fire aimed at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Later on in that day, did you see this person, Mr. Dragan Papic, again?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. After that, I managed to get out of there, but I saw him before that, but not after that, because within a relatively short time period, I managed to go to Stari Vitez, Vrhovine, I can explain that if you like, and from there I went to Zenica, and then I left for Tuzla. I began working for the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, let's remain with the 20th of October for the time being. When you saw Mr. Dragan Papic on the first floor of his house facing your house and firing into your home, at what time was it, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Between half past seven and eight. A long time has passed, so I can't remember exactly. So it could be an hour, more or less, because at moments like this, a person cannot know the exact moment when shots are being fired and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To the best of your memory, how long did the firing take place from Dragan Papic's house into your house? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, the first round of fire, and then perhaps for ten minutes, but not from the house anymore. It started from the wood behind the house, and from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You talked about firing that was made under the house; is that correct, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please specify on this photograph where these shots were coming from from under the house and how?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't see it from this angle, from this part here. This is in the way, this vegetation, which is like a fence, but it was here (indicating). This garage was built later. It wasn't there then, so it was behind this garage. I think this is a more recent photograph, and this wasn't here then. It was behind where this building is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you see the persons who were firing from the locations you just indicated to us?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told you who the persons were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please repeat it for us?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In that wood, there were several people, but as I was crawling along, I saw Dragan Papic, Pero Papic, Slavko and Rafael Milicevic, and a few other people. I didn't recognise the others, but they were all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To be perfectly clear, according to your own memory, Mr. Dragan Papic, first you saw him at his window; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the house, yes, yes, and then he went out and joined the others down there, but this was -- I left the house at about 4.15, so it was about eight hours later. It was during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us move on to the time in which you left your house with your children and family, your wife and also your mother-in-law. You indicated that you were carrying in your arms a child.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: ... mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you were carrying in your arms a child?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, under my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How old was this child at this time?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was born on the 28th of February, 1988, and that was on the 20th of October, '92, so he was about four years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You stated at that time that when you left the house, you came under fire.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The fire was aimed at me and my son, at my wife, but, no, they did not shoot at my wife and my female relatives, they were female persons. So I and my son were the ones they were shooting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, during that time, while you were leaving your house with your son, your four-year-old son, in your arms, where were the shots coming from, the ones that you had come under?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: From this direction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember the weapon or weapons that were used? What type of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was an anti-aircraft machine-gun and artillery automatic firearms, because there were rounds of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were not hit?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, luckily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could we consider then on the 20th of October, in any way possible could it have been a target that was -- a military one?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been a military target, because on that day I had no weapons there. I didn't shoot at all, I had no weapons at all, and I did not tend to carry firearms. I could have because of my duties, but I rarely used the weapons before the war. It was not a military target. After a certain time I'm trying to say that all the civilian population from Ahmici managed to withdraw from that part into the upper part of the village on the 20th of October, and I was the only one left there with my family. I realised that later when I went to the upper part and found them all there. Later I heard that Mr. Dario Kordic had stated on Vitez television, within Croatian television Vitez that on the 20th of October, in Ahmici, a Mujehadin military depot had been destroyed, and when I saw it on television I saw that they were showing my house. However, when things quieted down some 10 or 15 days later, my wife came back to take some personal belongings, what was left of them, what hadn't been burnt, and no one had entered the house. All the technical equipment was still there, the video, the TV set, the camera, it was all there. We managed to take all these things. This drama lasted from 8.00 a.m. until 4.00 p.m., and we had managed to put all these things into our business premises downstairs where we assume the fire would not reach, and some 10 or 15 days later, when things quieted down, my wife came back. I didn't go back to Ahmici after that, except for once incognito in this six-month interval. From October, 1992 until April, 1993 I only went there once surreptitiously, incognito, and then I didn't come again until a few months ago now that people have started returning to Ahmici and rebuilding their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What happened to your house after your departure, after the 20th of October, 1992? You indicated that it had not been searched, it had not been pillaged or plundered. Nonetheless, it was damaged?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The roof and the attic burnt completely, and the corridor, the children's bedroom and the pantry were gutted, but there was a big living-room and kitchen,. And because it started to rain, this was charred, but the rain had put out the fire, because just before we left it started to rain, to pour, in fact. And I know that after we left the house no one entered the house. Our house was not looted. We found all our technical equipment, because my wife's sister and my wife came back and they took all this. I spent some time in Vrhovina when I went to Stari Vitez. I was helped by Dr. Mosinovic, and my family and I were taken there in an ambulance, and then we stayed in Stari Vitez where he was protected, because they asked for my extradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic I would like to show you then two photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, your house -- is your house visible in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: This is my house. You can see it from this -- the signpost here. There is even a sign here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, this commercial sign that is very clear, this yellow sign with the red letters, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was put up after the end of the conflict. It says, "Papic Car Waste". He was selling car parts, and now there are old abandoned vehicles there. I spent a few months there, and I can see that they're doing well. Muslims and Croats come to buy here. Because the house is being repaired, I had to clean this and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then that sign, that commercial advertisement, did not exist at the time of the event in October?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. It was put up later, because he didn't have this then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you do -- where did you go after the 20th of October, 1992? What did you do after that time period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: After I managed to get out alive, I went to Esad Ahmic's house in the upper part of Ahmici on the 20th of October, in the evening. I spent the night there. I was wearing the clothes I had on but I was barefoot. We spent the night there, and in the morning, at about 5.00, half past five, we went in the direction of Vrhovina. Vrhovina is a village above Ahmici. I spent a short time, I don't know exactly how long. I stayed in the house of the mother of a doctor who was my friend. He was a medical practitioner in Vitez. He was highly esteemed, and we -- he found out that his mother was having heart trouble. He went to visit her. And when he came, I told him that I would have to go to Stari Vitez with my family, and the next day he arrived with an ambulance, and my wife, my children, my wife's sister and my mother-in-law got in, and because there was a HVO checkpoint and they had requested my extradition as a criminal who allegedly dug up the Catholic graves in the Ahmici graveyard, I was afraid. So they wrapped me up in pillow cases and white sheets, and they put me in the boot. And that's how I passed through the checkpoint and arrived in Stari Vitez. Since I had worked in the Municipality of Stari Vitez, taking care of the refugees from Eastern Bosnia and from Krajina, and I worked in the Civil Defence Department, so I set up contacts, because the first UNHCR office in Bosnia was opened in Vitez in the Bombac (Phoen) building. And then the head, who was a Dane and with whom I had established contact previously and who visited in my house and we had become friends, he later told me that he had cried when he heard my house was on fire. Well, he managed to find me after a month, a month and a half, and he asked me how I was making a living, what I was doing. And I said I was in hiding, that I was living off humanitarian aid, that I was like a refugee. He asked me -- or, rather, he offered me a job in the Logistics Department. He said I could be his driver. I thought he was joking, but he was serious. So the next day I showed up for work and I was his driver. Until December we were in Vitez and he insisted that I should go to Zenica, because he had obtained some information since Ivica Santic was the head of the municipality and he was on good terms with him, as I was, and he learned there was a possibility that the HVO could either kill me or blow up the vehicle, so he insisted that I should go to Zenica. So the whole office, in fact, moved to Zenica, and we stayed in Zenica until the 21st of January, 1993. From there we went to Tuzla, where I felt safer, because I wanted to be as far away as possible. I remained in Tuzla until the end of 1994 covering the Tuzla area for the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993 you were in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And Tuzla is located in the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How far, approximately, is it located from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Oh, it was very far then, because you had to go by forest roads through Milankovic because roads were blocked, and it was then I passed along this route for the first time. And this road was about 221 kilometres long, and the normal road is about 100 kilometres or so through Nova Gracica. Then on the 16th of April I was in Tuzla, and in the office I read on the printer, as far as I could read English, that something had happened in Ahmici. And then my boss came and asked me if I had anyone in Ahmici. He said it had been very bad there on the 16th of April, and I said that my -- some of my relatives were there, and my wife. And I asked what was happening, and he told me that he would give me all the information he knew. But then I requested leave to go to Zenica to see whether they were alive. I was given the use of a vehicle, an official vehicle, an Nissan Jeep. It was snowing. I came to Zenica because my wife and children were staying in a flat in Zenica. I asked them whether they knew anything, and they said I knew more than they did. I stayed for two days, and I learned that my brother had gone to Stari Vitez with his family where my sister was, and my mother happened to be visiting my sister in Vitez that day. And the rest of the family, I learned that they were no longer alive simply. And then I came back to Tuzla on the 20th of April, and I returned to my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you meet a certain number of your family members in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the ones who managed to get out. There were two collective centres where they could stay, my closest relatives who had managed to get out. My wife took them food, clothing, any help we could give them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your family members tell you what had happened in April in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, will you just hold a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, although we don't have any rule against the hearsay evidence, I wonder whether we could move on, because we are not -- we are going to hear other evidence about what happened on the 16th of April, so I don't need -- I don't think we need to hear the evidence about -- the hearsay evidence from this witness about the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, since 1993, have you ever returned to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of months ago. Houses are being rebuilt. The first 35 houses are being rebuilt by -- with the help of international aid, and mine is one of them. So I have been there since April this year. Before that I didn't go, only when I went to visit with delegations like Mr. Garnic (Phoen), for instance, because for the first time of office I was president of the Municipal Council in Vitez. After the Washington Agreement was signed between the Bosniaks and Croats, I was president of the Legislative Branch, and Mr. Lacovic Franjo (Phoen) was the president of the other branch. We worked very well, we opened the roads, the communication lines, water and electricity supplies. I am in Ahmici, and my family because our house is being rebuilt. But I have to state in court that the overall situation is good, but still, individual incidents occur, and I think that Goran Papic, for instance, I had problems with him a couple of times. He would intercept my car last year, and we had some unpleasant encounters. On one occasion he tried to hit my son with a car. He jumped into the ditch to save himself, because he didn't know who it was that was trying to hit him with a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who Goran Papic is?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Goran Papic is Dragan Papic's brother, the son of Ivo Papic, who is the owner of this automobile scrap yard, so that we are still exposed to provocations. Not just me and not just by Goran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, do you feel that these events here are pertinent to the facts that concern us in this trial, what is going on right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do believe that this concerns the Tribunal, which is part of all of the evidence that we're going to be presenting and is of interest to this Tribunal to know what has happened and what is presently the case of the relations between the Croats and Muslim residents of Ahmici. I'm not saying that this is in the very heart of our trial as such, but nonetheless, this is a bit of information which may not be completely useless to this Tribunal, of course. The Tribunal will make use of it as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We may indeed look at the general climate, the general atmosphere which now prevails in Ahmici, but without mentioning, perhaps, any specific names or any persons, particularly if these persons may be linked to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I do not envisage posing any more questions on this particular aspect of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, is Dragan Papic in this room?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you please indicate to us in what location he is in this room?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the last row. He is the first one, the one with the beard. Do I have to point a finger at him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's not necessary. Mr. President, I have one last photograph I would like to submit and show to the witness, which is quite different from the one that's already been presented to the witness. It is simply a photograph of his house.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Exhibit 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could you please indicate your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It is the same photograph as before, but from a slightly different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. I request that Exhibits 59, 60 and 61 be tendered as Prosecution exhibits, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. I see there is no objection to the various exhibits, and I turn now -- I will turn now to Mr. Pavkovic to ask him whether he can indicate to us which Defence counsel are going to cross-examine our witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: The witness, Mr. President -- good morning, first of all. The witness will be cross-examined by attorney Petar Puliselic, followed by attorney Ranko Radovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you mentioned that in October, 1992, from the direction of Busovaca, Fojnica and other places, HV units were on the move, going in the direction of Novi Travnik, in order to assist HVO forces there who were engaged in conflict with the BiH army in that area, and that that was the reason why a roadblock was put up in Ahmici, to prevent the passage of those units. You said that the HVO had falsely claimed that it wanted to assist its forces in the area of Jajce, where fighting was going on against the Serbs. My question is: How do you know that the HVO did not, in fact, intend to go to Jajce? Were the reports you got verified?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: When you say -- use the word "Listopad" would you please use a word that I understand too, October. Secondly, it was not the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And thirdly, I had firsthand information. I checked them, I said that I was a member of the highest level leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether at the time there was fighting in Jajce between the forces of Republika Srpska and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the area of Jajce, Republika Srpska did not exist, so it was the aggression of the Serb forces and the defence forces of Jajce which meant the Bosniaks and the Croats were together at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who won in those battles, what happened with Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask not to be asked such questions, because I haven't come here because of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But this is linked to my next questions.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Jajce fell. The defence forces did not succeed in defending it. I'm answering the question. The defence forces did not manage to defend it and Jajce fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if one goes from Busovaca towards Jajce, does one have to pass through Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: From Busovaca to Jajce if you're going by road, I know you pass through Ahmici, Vitez, Travnik and across Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So you have to pass through Travnik to get to Jajce. Is there any other road, and if there is another road, will you tell us which is the shortest route to Jajce from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 20th of October, 1992, you were in your home in Ahmici, together with your family, when the HVO attack started in the early morning and continued on into the afternoon. In the statement that you gave to the investigator of the International Tribunal, you said that your house was targeted from the direction of Hrasno with anti-aircraft guns and also from the wood south of Papic's house. You also said that at the time you saw Dragan Papic shooting an automatic rifle from the window of his house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Now you claim that the fire started from Dragan Papic's house with an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: That's what I said the first time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You now claim something that you didn't mention at all last time, and that is that Dragan Papic was using a PAT?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, a PUM. There's a difference, a PAT being an anti-aircraft gun and PUM being an anti-aircraft machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You didn't mentioned that in your previous statement. Also you said that around the anti-aircraft machine gun there were other people, other neighbours of yours who were Croats. This is something you also failed to mention in your previous statement. Could you tell us with precision where this PUM, anti-aircraft machine gun, was positioned?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the wood behind Ivo Papic's house. I've already shown you that on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In your testimony today, you said that Dragan Papic used an automatic rifle to shoot with, and then after that you said that you think it was Dragan Papic. Are you quite sure who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Maybe I made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But that has entered the transcript. Can you tell us who it was that opened the shutters on your window?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: On one window, it was my wife, on the other, me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Was it simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Who was the first to open the shutters when the fire was open?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I was the first one to open the shutters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something else today for the first time. For instance, you said that on the window of the house of Dragan Papic, there were sandbags?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Halfway up the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How high up is that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: There are various sizes of windows. I didn't measure the window, but it went halfway up the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Very well. How, then, could you see that Dragan Papic was wearing a black uniform if the sandbags went halfway up the window?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Dragan Papic was wearing a black uniform for three or four months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you said that you saw him then wearing a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I saw him wearing a black cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What kind of a cap was it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was a black cap with a rim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you said you saw him wearing a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: But I saw him this way, this far up, his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Now you said for the first time that after the round of fire from the automatic rifle that fire started from other weapons. I've already mentioned that, that is, the discrepancy between what you said today and your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I'd like to see that statement. I don't know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: It is the statement you gave to the investigator of the International Tribunal, when was it, let me see, on the 17th of November, '97 and the 9th of December, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it back to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us whether this is your signature? Could the usher show a copy of the statement to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 1/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Probably that particular document carries the comments, personal comments, of one of the Defence counsel. I wonder whether we could take it as an exhibit. I'm asking the Defence counsel who provided it to Mr. Puliselic, the copy, whether he's prepared to provide us with that copy so that it can be regarded as an exhibit? Did you write anything on that document? Mr. Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we gave my learned colleague a copy of this statement from our files, and we don't mind that it should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. May I answer the question put to me by Mr. Puliselic? This statement is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I can show it to you in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Can I have it in Bosnian, please, so that I can see the discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I didn't have an English copy so I borrowed it from my colleague Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D1/5A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Puliselic, could you please indicate to the witness the page and the lines where there's a discrepancy in his statement, the particular place where, in your view, there's a discrepancy between what he said here in court and what he declared to the Prosecutor's investigators in '97?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has both documents now. I don't have anything on me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have the Bosnian text, but may I quote it? "On the morning, artillery fire was opened with an anti-artillery gun from the direction of Hrasno which is two or three kilometres away. At that time, I saw Dragan Papic, the son of Ivo Papic, shooting from an automatic rifle from the window of his house."

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was just saying that in that statement you didn't mention the fact that Dragan Papic started shooting and that after him came the fire from other weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: That is not what you said, but I don't want to argue with you. You just said that there was a discrepancy. I said what I said, and please let it be entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Puliselic, could we move on to your further question because now this point has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you claim that you saw Papic in the wood, as well as other neighbours of yours, Croats, and that you saw Papic using the anti-aircraft machine gun. Can you explain how come Dragan Papic can manage all that, first to fire from the window, then simultaneously comes the fire from the wood, and then later you see him in the wood? Could you tell us what is the distance between your house and the wood?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that this happened at the same time. I made it clear that this period was from 7.30 in the morning until late afternoon. The exact time when he shot at me and my son from the anti-aircraft machine gun was about 4.00 in the afternoon when I tried to manage to save myself and my son. As I was crawling, I saw him, his partners, his house, and his weapon, because the ground on my side is a little higher than where his house is. So one person cannot be in two places at once. Let me make myself clear. I said that this first act happened at eight in the morning and the second at four in the afternoon. The distance between my house and Dragan Papic's house is 60 to 80 metres, that is, we are separated by the main road. And the wood is about 150 metres from my house, and from Dragan's house, 80 to 90 metres. Of course, this is an approximation. I may be 10, 20 metres wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you only just said this time that it was in the afternoon at 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I made it quite clear that this was a period from the morning until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Puliselic, I think the witness is right. However, if you don't mind, I would like him to clarify a point. I know he said that in the afternoon at around 4.00, he saw Dragan Papic shooting at him when he was carrying his son in his arm. I wonder whether you could say whether this is exactly what you intended to say, namely, that you saw him shooting at you, because previously I think you said that there was some shooting from a particular area near Mr. Papic's house. At 4.00, did you see Mr. Papic shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Not just Mr. Papic, but all of them, they were all shooting at me, and he was shooting from the machine gun. I said that the shells made holes in the grass that were this size, so that the calibre was quite considerable. I went zig-zag, and I had some crazy luck. God protected me and I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you were escaping from the back side of your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In what direction were you moving when you left your house? In what direction?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Could I have the photograph, please, the photograph of my house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It would be 60 or 61. Which one would you like to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't mind, either. This one will do fine.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: So you see, I wasn't moving behind the house. My entrance is on this side. The entrance to my house is this side. This is the front facade, so from a door which was on the right-hand side, and my own car was parked there, so I crawled behind it, below the fence, across this meadow to my uncle's house here. And that is when they started firing from the wood. Then from there, I crossed another road going to Ahmici, to the house of Pezer Omer, and then further up to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you see from there who is shooting from the wood and who is manning the anti-aircraft machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Of course you can. It's about 100 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But it's in the wood?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. It is at the beginning of the wood. It wasn't among the trees. It was just at the beginning of the wood behind the house. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, can you tell us whether, previous to this event on the 20th of October, there was a roadblock in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October? I was asking before that, a month before that or something like that, earlier on, were there any barricades near your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Near my house, no. In front of my house, no, possibly near the cemetery or near Pican's cafe. There were many checkpoints in those days, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you recall one occasion when you attended a birthday party of a little girl, Rafael Milicevic's daughter, and that you used your camera to film the party?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the same way that I filmed the wedding of Mr. Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I should like to tell you that we have been told that the day after that event, this barricade was put up near your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: This was on the 30th of September, 1992, the birthday party, so the next day on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Not in front of my house but a little lower down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So a little lower down from your house. Do you know Marijan Jukic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I know two Marijan Jukics. I don't know which one you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the one working in the police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: This Marijan Jukic, when this roadblock was put up a little way from your house, did he come to see you and ask you to remove the barricade?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that he did come and some other people, but I wasn't alone. There was Leyman (phoen) Ahmic, so I can't remember whether he personally asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It is possible. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you remove the barricade? Was it removed after he came?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is linked to this event. Not when he came, but after that, the roadblock was removed, before night-time anyway. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you have a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you own any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I had official weapons, but not at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Where did you have it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: In the party, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you ever bring these weapons home?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, because of the children. They were little.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: The Defence has information that you fired shots from your house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No. Did anyone see me shoot?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: At whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you shoot at Goran Papic when he was still a small boy?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, never. These are insinuations. I said I never carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Due to the event I have mentioned and you are denying, did Papic, on one occasion in Vitez, talk to you about this?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Which Papic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Dragan. When he met you on one occasion, did he complain about this?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I never met Dragan Papic and we never talked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that you were employed by the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did there?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I was the driver of Mr. Anders Levison, a Dane. I was his personal driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How long did you work in UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Until 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I left because I had to feed my family and for reasons of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: No. I mean, why did you leave the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Why did I leave it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes. What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Because a new boss arrived, my old boss left. I came back to Zenica to work in the UNHCR office there. I didn't get on well with the boss there who was Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were ever sentenced?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Not for a crime but for misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to criminal offences, ten, fifteen years ago?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't. There was a trial where I was on probation, but I was never sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you at one time belong to an organisation called the Young Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I suggest we now take a break before moving on to counsel Radovic and Pavkovic. I would like to thank the accused for accepting to have a short break. I understand you agreed that we should only have a 15-minute break so that we may try to finish the cross-examination, the re-examination, if any, of the present witness. We will have a short recess of only 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, first Mr. Pavkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Today I will be the last to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. Good day, Mr. Ahmic, I'm attorney Petar Pavkovic. First of all, let us understand one another. I am using the language I usually use. As you can see, we have interpreters here. I hope that we will understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I hope so too, but if you are mentioning the names of months, I don't know the Croatian names of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have consideration on this point. Mr. Ahmic, according to the material at the disposal of the Defence counsel, we can see that as regards the events you are testifying to today, you are speaking about them for the first time after five years to the Prosecution investigators. Can you tell me how it came about that you are here as a witness to these events?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It is not true that I am talking about this for the first time. I made the statement to our ORGS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the information the Defence counsel have at their disposal, not the information you have at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I made a statement, as soon as I left Ahmici, to our bodies, to our security bodies, and it is not the first time I'm speaking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When I draw your attention to this point, I have to clarify. I'm doing this because my questions will partly rely on the statements you have made today, and partly on what you said in the statement presented to attorney Puliselic, which you have before you, I believe. Mr. Ahmic, you were one of the founders of the Party of Democratic Action. You held a high position in that party, you were deputy president at one time, you said you were president, and evidently, you had access to information about political relations in the area of Vitez, especially Ahmici. I would like to know what your views were and are on the inter-ethnic relations, the relations between the Croats and the Bosniaks, the development of these relations, but briefly, from the first conflict which took place on the 20th of October, 1992. You talked about your relations with Mr. Papic and the other Croats in the village, but how do you view the overall relations, in brief?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The part of Central Bosnia in which I live, the Vitez municipality of the Ahmici village, the relations between these two nations and the third nation, the Serbs, and the 2.000 majority population were exceptionally well, good, and in the period that we are talking about, there were no special ethnic problems. As I learned from my father, the relations in the previous war were quite good. There is a bright example where Jur Savidovic saved my father in that war, because an army came by and he hid him in his barn. And he said, "If you think there's someone in my barn, you can set fire to me and the barn". So he saved my father's life, and they were on very good terms. Relations after the multi-party elections and after the establishment of, let us call them conditionally, the national parties, were very good. I believe, you know, that we had a coalition before the first multi-party elections, until Boban, Mr. Mate Boban, became the head of the Croatian side, while Mr. Kilica was the head and or Mr. Perinkovic, or whatever his name was, I forget, before that we cooperated extremely well. We established the joint government bodies. We agreed on the distribution of positions, some posts were reserved for Croats, others for Muslims. The police commander, for example, was a Bosniak. So the cooperation, both at the Federal -- at the State level and at the local level were very good. I will not elaborate, but this was how it was, until the HDZ changed its policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, could we limit ourselves to the period up to the 20th? Mr. Boban became the head of the HDZ after October, 1992. Is there anything else you can say about these relations?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're referring to politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the overall relations, the political and the inter-ethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, up to June or July, 1992, relations were quite good, because you know, that we offered joint resistance in Noposivina, Western Bosnia, Brcko, Eastern Bosnia and so on, Herzegovina. There was joint resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you waged the war together?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I will not press this point any further. Let us be more specific now and go back to the event of the 20th of October, 1992. You stated that on that day or the day before, you had received an order from the Territorial Defence staff in Vitez that you should set up a roadblock in Ahmici on the Busovaca/Vitez road. Can you tell me who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't receive an order, because I was not a soldier. It was an instruction, which was a political instruction, and it was the army that issued orders to members of the army. I was above them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So who received information that roadblocks should be set up?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It was the leader of the army in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you find this out about from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I found out from the wartime presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Who, if you know, organised the men manning the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Territorial Defence headquarters staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, as we were told in the army, that a barricade is not a barricade if it is not defended? How did you expect this barricade to be defended if you say you were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The way you ask this question -- I was not taught that in the army. I was a cook in the JNA, and they didn't teach me how to set up roadblocks. But you cannot compare the JNA with the army that we had, the jointly and then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. You said that there were no weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I said there were very few weapons. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, furthermore, who was at the head of this group of armed villagers, as you call it, that organised the setting up of this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that Muris Ahmic, my cousin, was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed. Can you tell me, Mr. Ahmic, I am going back to that morning of October, the early morning, you said that shots had been aimed at your house, that after that your house was set on fire and that other Muslim Bosniak houses were not damaged at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't say they were not damaged. Shots were aimed at the other Muslim houses as well, but I said they were not torched, except for my house and a part of the house of Hajrudin Pjanic I think was torched. And I said that some stables or cow sheds had been burnt, and some hay-stacks, because I saw that from my house. This was around my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, you said that you hid behind the stairs with your family?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The entrance, the stairway at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did this face toward the area from where you say the shots came?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, it was sideways.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a view of the place from which shots were coming?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You kept the door open?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How could you then notice where the shots were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see through that door, I could only see it from upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you went downstairs immediately after the shots started.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I just left my children there, and then I went back upstairs because my telephone was there and we wanted to take our technical equipment and put it away in a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Ahmic. You said that you are no longer a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you leave the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: That's my personal decision. I went to -- I joined another party, which I find more acceptable now, and this is the party for Bosnia-Herzegovina led by Mr. Haris Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you say that the new party has the same political platform as the SDA, that it is advocating an independent and democratic Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But now you've said something different.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: What did I say that's different?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You should know.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean? I joined the party called The Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a democratic multi-national, multi-ethnic party, fighting for an independent, free democratic Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDA has the same idea, the same principles, but the methods are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That's your interpretation, but let the matter rest there. Can you tell me -- let us go back to this roadblock. You received information that the roadblock should be set up on the road near your house. Then you said that you sought out certain people, and that you asked them that this roadblock should be moved toward the road. Who did you contact?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I contacted the president of the command of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you do this as a civilian rather than a military person?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Because it was my house and the house of Ivo Papic that were in question. I didn't want the roadblock to be set up between the two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the aim of the setting up of the roadblock was to prevent the forces of the HVO, to prevent them from proceeding toward, as you say, Novi Travnik or Jajce. You prevented them, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't say they were forces of the Croatian army. You said the HVO, which is correct. And secondly, yes, they were prevented -- or rather, they were not prevented but they were delayed because if they had been prevented, my house wouldn't have been burnt down and the village wouldn't have been evacuated and so on. About 20 or so hours elapsed, and at this time they were prevented from moving in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: This would correspond with what you said previously, that they managed to break through your defence?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not the defence but the checkpoint which prevented the passage of civilians, goods and the army.
