utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I go back to the material which attorney Petar Puliselic has attended to show the witness that they broke through their defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: This is material which the witness has in front of him. Will you please look at page 2. Page 2, toward the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we set up a roadblock. There were only 20 of us. The HVO managed to break through the defence. Well, it wasn't a defence. Perhaps that's the word used here. The HVO managed to break our defence and move towards Novi Travnik. Well, if someone sets up a checkpoint they have to defend themselves at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said you had been a cook?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, some things are evident even to a cook, if they're logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I would like to ask you to clarify, once again, how it is possible that you carried a four-year-old child under your arm, crawling, hiding from fire and at the same time you were able to observe so carefully as to notice even the kind of clothing worn by people a hundred metres away from you at the beginning of a wood. I believe that while retreating, you were hiding behind certain obstacles which would provide protection from the firing. If that is so, how were you able to see what you say you saw?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: What you have just said, that you can observe, crawl and save your child all at the same time is correct. I ask you, if you had been in the same situation as me, would you have done all this too? In the period from 8.00 a.m. until 4.00 p.m. to be precise is a period of eight hours, and within this period I was both upstairs in my house from which I had a very good view of the surroundings, and I was able to see all these people several times. And when I left my house my car, an Opal Record, was parked, and when I open the door the first time there was a burst of fire. When I opened my door the second time there was no firing, so I was able to go out. I hid behind my car for a while, and observing. And then when I went out into the open, I crawled zigzag. There were no obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, my last question to

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You explained, Mr. Ahmic, the following: That the firing was aimed at you, but that your wife, your daughter, your mother-in-law were not shot at, if I understood you correctly. In other words, the aim of this alleged attack was not to shoot at other civilians, but only you personally?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stated and I still maintain that the women civilians were not shot at, and that is the absolute truth. It's not the alleged truth. They shot only at me and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I say "allegedly" because you say it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I shall be very direct. If you personally were the target of the people shooting at you, why did you take a four-year-old child, instead of letting your wife take care of the child, as she was not exposed to fire?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I ask you whether your wife or your mother-in-law or your wife's sister would be capable of taking care of a small child who was terrified and shivering from fright, because they had experienced all the fire and the shots that had hit the house before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is not the answer to my question, because I'm sure your child would have felt just as safe with his mother as he did with you. My question is: Why didn't the mother take the child when the mother was not exposed to fire, but it was you who took the child and you were a target?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Probably under present-day circumstances, I would have probably given him to his mother, but in those circumstances, I never thought about it. I was six years married, and she had six miscarriages, after a pregnancy of four or five months. I never thought about it. I took the boy with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the investigator of the Prosecution, you didn't describe in the same way the fire of the anti-aircraft machine gun, but you said, literally, the HVO was using anti-aircraft machine guns from the direction of the wood that was behind the house of Ivo Papic, the father of Dragan; is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Could you show me where it says that? Do you have the Croatian translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian one. It's all the same. Let's not insist. As much as you love your Croatian language, I love mine, but let's not argue about that. That is least important. So if you have the translation, it would be on the third page, if we have the same translation, the tenth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in the statement. I have now made it even clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that is what you told the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, if it says so in the statement, but today I have clarified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I see. You have clarified it. How come you're able to clarify a statement when more time has elapsed since the event than at the time you were giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Dragan Papic is not a member of the HVO, then he is not. If Pero Papic is not, if he is not a member of the HVO at the time, then he didn't fire, and here I'm talking about a group of people. Dragan was shooting with the anti-aircraft machine gun, and the others were using infantry weapons, and I think I was quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe that anti-aircraft machine gun that was being used by Dragan Papic? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It's three-barrelled. It has a seat. I saw it the night before and a couple of days before that. At one point, it was mounted on a Tam lorry, and at this time it was on a stand, but I know it is a PUM, an anti-aircraft machine gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I still haven't quite understood your description. Where is the ammunition on this gun, on this machine gun?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: On the top in a magazine. That's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: With three-barrelled guns it's in a magazine?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: It is where the trigger is. I've told you. I didn't go close up to it to examine it. I could see it from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But the ammunition, is it in a kind of round case for this kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But I am telling you --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't go up to it to see it properly, but I saw it from a certain distance, from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How far is it from your house to Papic Dragan's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I said about 60 to 80 metres, and from the wood to my house, 100 to 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, but I think "refugee" is the wrong word. He's an exile. He has been exiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he just came to visit his family, so what term should be used? This witness, who was a protected witness, claims that the weapon was a different weapon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You should have not mentioned his name. We will have a redaction. I will ask the registrar if she could prefer the relevant form to be filled in. Please refrain from mentioning any names of protected witnesses. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I realised my mistake when I had made it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: There is a description of a different weapon in connection with Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Could you please spare me the distortions. I don't know what this gentleman said, and I don't know what knowledge he has of weapons. I gave a concise statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But he was not a cook. He was a person dealing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Don't insist on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He has already said what his position is. I mean, there's no point in continuing with this matter. Could you move on to your next question, please? You have made your point, namely, the inconsistency between two witnesses, according to you, what you consider an inconsistency between two witnesses. Now we can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with you, even though this question was meant to test the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, what significance the black uniform has for you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of mentioning a black uniform or, rather, what does the fact that somebody wears a black uniform mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The black uniform was the uniform worn by people who belonged to the Black Shirt movement. As far as I know from the previous war, these were members of the Ustasha movement who committed crimes. I'm old enough to have studied this in history, at least the history I was taught in those days, and that uniform was worn by members of the Ustasha movement, a fascist movement, during the independent state of Croatia. The uniform worn by Dragan Papic had on one side the HVO and on the other the letter "U," and on his cap, he had the letter "U" which means Ustasha. And the associations were very bad for us, not just for me, but for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So that according to what you said, all members of the Ustasha army wore a black uniform? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: You're asking me as if I was at a history lesson. The independent state of Croatia, I think, had a regular army known as the Home Guards, and these were special units, as far as I studied history, but I don't think this is a history lesson.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My question is whether all the Ustashas wore a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: They may have not all worn black uniforms, but they were fascists, proclaimed as fascists by the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because black uniforms were worn only by members of the Black Legion, but let's not go into the details.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: We used to referred to them as "black shirt wearers." I'm telling you what the association is in Central Bosnia among the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, your father Adem, during World War II, was he a member of any army?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think he was a member, because at the time it was the independent state of Croatia, he was a member of the Home Guards. He was captured by the Germans, at least that is what he told me. He was held in captivity in Germany for a certain period of time, I can't remember now, because my father died quite a long time ago. Then he escaped from there and returned to the former Yugoslavia, to Bosnia, and after that I know that he told me that he was with Ivo Kupreskic as a member of the reserve force after 1945, and that is Zoran and Mirjan's uncle and he was serving in Nis. I don't know why you're asking me things about my father. He was not a member of any Muslim army. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My question was to see if he was a member of any SS division?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were never convicted, but you said that you were given a sentence on parole, a suspended sentence. Will you tell us what you were found guilty of?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: When I said that, I'm not ashamed of it. I don't want to hide it. Each individual has his own history file. I was working in a cafe, the infamous Bungalow in 1974/1975. I was a waiter. I think it was in 1975, there was a fight or, rather, a drunken guest came. He tried to attack me, and my owner, the proprietor, his name was Jovo, he drew a knife at me. We threw out this drunken guest. My boss at the time was apparently working in the state security. I didn't even know that. He tied him up. He took him to the police station in Vitez. After that, I was summoned to court as an accomplice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: For bodily injury?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, for participation in the fight. So I was given a suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what kind of an offence it was. Indeed, it was nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I was never convicted of any other offences, except traffic offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When this shooting occurred on the 20th of October, do you know whether Drago Josipovic's stable was burned as well?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know because he lives in another part of the village. I don't know. I never heard anything about it. It's possible. I have no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm not asking you to say anything you don't know. Do you know anything about the village of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know where it is. I don't know what you want to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What was the majority population?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: According to the '91 census, I think that two-thirds were Serbs and one-third Bosniaks, roughly. I'm not quite sure, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the Serbs in that village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The Serbs from that village left with the assistance of the Vitez HVO. They were dislocated or, rather, moved to the present-day territory of Republika Srpska, and they gave up their homes and things in order to be moved from there. On one occasion, I visited Tolovici, together with Pero Skopljak and Mr. Novica Mijatovic who was the president of the SDS at the time, and we tried to calm down the people, to persuade them not to move out. I mentioned the three of us because we were the political leaders of the political parties at the time. We tried to prevent it. Afterwards, they didn't go collectively, but they moved out one by one, but there are some people from Tolovici still living in Vitez, but they didn't remain in the party under the control of the Bosnian authorities, the army, but under the party, under the control of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Why did the Serbs move out of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know the motive, but I know as a minority people, they were probably afraid of some kind of retaliation, because Kupres fell at the time, you know what happened at Kupres, what happened at Ravno, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigator of the Tribunal, you said that Pero Skopljak was the head of police, the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: The chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know until when?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that he was until the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What date do you have in mind, the 20th of October or the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that he was chief of police on the 20th of October. No, on the 16th of April, he wasn't for sure, because it was Mirko Samija, my school friend, personal friend, who unfortunately got killed, a judge from Travnik. So Mirko Samija was the chief of police on the 16th of April because the HVO took away my Golf, and through my friends in Kiseljak, I tried to restore it. But unfortunately, the conflict occurred on the 16th, but I don't know until when he was chief of police. I know that from the moment the coalition government was formed between the HDZ and the SDA, Pero Skopljak was head of the police and Saban Mahmutovic was a police unit leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My question was the date.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Sakib Ahmic whose family got killed in central Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I know three Sakib Ahmics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But everyone knows Sakib Ahmic whose son was killed, daughter-in-law, and two grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: My uncle Sakib Ahmic, his son and his wife were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm interested in Sakib Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Son of Dervis or son of Mehmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Son of Dervis.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, as far as I understand, you were in Tuzla. Did you have occasion to watch TV programmes in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I did, but I didn't watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't watch it at all?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I worked until very late, until 10.00, 11.00, sometimes 12.00, because eastern Bosnia was falling. The UNHCR had to go to Brcko, Banovici, Teocak, and so on and so forth. I apologise. Let me just say that I heard about Ahmici on the UNHCR telex, on the printer that the UNHCR had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone that people were shown on television who had managed to escape from Ahmici and who ended up in the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I heard that later when I reached Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel be asked to slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier, any further examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, a few clarifications. The first one deals with the sentence that Mr. Ahmic had. I think there was some clarification that is necessary with regard to the translation

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It was stated in the transcript, "Were you ever sentenced?" Response, "Not for a crime but for misdemeanours." Perhaps a clarification should be made with a response from Mr. Ahmic. Mr. Ahmic, you were only convicted once; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was just this one fight, shall we call it. That is what the court defined it as, so participation in a fight. This was only once, and I got a suspended sentence as a participant in this fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How old were you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it was 1975, so I was about 20. I was working as a waiter in that restaurant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, getting back to a question put by Mr. Radovic, it seemed that there are some contradictions that were raised between a statement made by another witness and the statement made by Mr. Ahmic made before this Tribunal. Mr. Ahmic, do you know what type of contradiction this may be with regards to the weapon described by the other witness and the event of April 1993? All the weapons that you described were seen by you in October 1992. Did you understand the supposed contradiction that was raised by Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. President. On the 19th of October, at what distance from the roadblock, which was erected on the road, was your house located?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it can be shown on the photograph. The roadblock was next to the cemetery, and the distance between the cemetery and my house, I'm not very good at estimating distances, but maybe 500, 600 metres, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a consequence, could we reasonably state then that the fire, the shots which were fired upon your house, could not have been aimed at the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED AHMIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Ahmic, thank you for coming to court to testify. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, let me point out that today I had the impression that, in a way, through the notion of credibility of witnesses, Defence counsel were using a sort of Pandora's box. Many questions have been put which, although formally speaking, address the question of credibility of the witness, but were questions which should have been put by the Defence counsel of one particular accused, the one who had been mentioned by the witness, not the other Defence counsel. I think we are going to take a strict view of this notion of credibility of witnesses, and this will apply a fortiori when we move on to Prosecution witnesses who refer specifically to events which took place on the 16th of April and who refer, in particular, to one or more of the accused. Because otherwise, all Defence counsel will be allowed to put a lot of questions which, as I say, should, in principle, be put by the Defence counsel of the targeted accused. Let me now ask the Prosecution whether they have a list of witnesses they intend to call next week so that the Defence counsel know in advance what witnesses are going to be called here. We have now your document filed on the 19th of August on page 6, paragraph 5, we have a list of 13 witnesses. Are you going to stick to that list? So far we have heard four plus, of course, the expert witness, Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the list which was submitted in the early part of this week and was submitted to the Defence, as well as to this Tribunal, is still in force in that the witnesses we have called, we believe, may be heard during the course of this particular week. But, of course, now that we see that it cannot be done, it will be done next week. But we will be in a position to extend this list and we will do so. With the witnesses that are left, I believe that among those witnesses that are left to be heard, we believe that several days of hearing will be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So these are nine witnesses. I see that there are nine witnesses beginning with number 4, and then there's number 5, and Monday we will begin with that one; is that right? I'm not sure if he's protected or not, so I'm trying to avoid naming these witnesses. But then we can then continue with 6, 7, et cetera, in that order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There are nine then, I see. Perhaps you might also call on other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, in that case, you will tell us which witnesses this will involve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Mr. President, but it seems that already those witnesses that are going to come that have already been announced, we already see several days of hearings before us. Nonetheless, we will, indeed, inform the Defence in an appropriate time in advance of any further witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: With regards, you remember that there were ten witnesses for which there are no witness statements, and I asked you to submit to us a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. This was done. It's in the course of being transmitted to you. I believe it has been transmitted to the registrar or is in the process of being transmitted, as well as to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions? I wonder whether the legal counsel would like to raise any issue before we rise now, any issue relating to what we're going to do next week? Let me then wind up our hearing by saying that I would again stress the appeal we made to the Prosecution to try to shorten the list of those witnesses who only address Count 1. I had counted about 32. I wonder whether some of them have dropped out already. Probably some of the 32 have dropped out of the list of those who are not coming, but I wonder whether you could also shorten this list further. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are continually re-evaluating the state of the evidence and making decisions, almost on a daily basis, as to how best to streamline this case. I think there will be some reductions in the number of witnesses. I just feel I cannot end this session without expressing some concern about some things that happened earlier during cross-examination, and I think I will be asking for some opportunity to voice those concerns, perhaps, in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the mentioning of the name of the protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But this was a slip of a tongue. Of course, this may happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think that's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But that's why we have the special procedure for redaction. It happens. I mean, it's unintentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you not have a word with Defence counsel about this and explain the rules to them carefully? It's the sort of matter which, I should have thought, could be dealt with between counsel. They are not going to be familiar with our rules. Clearly, it is an unfamiliar procedure, and perhaps a quiet word might well solve the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think that's a good suggestion, and I certainly was under the assumption that they fully understood the rules of the game, and maybe that is a mistake on my part, not to have understood that. My concern was the raising of the name in a context where clearly there was no need to raise it. The testimony had no connection with what this witness was saying, and the time lapse between what this witness knew about and what the other witness knew about was at least two to three months. It appeared to me that there was a deliberate attempt to put that name out into the public gallery where there was press. Everyone knows that in this case, one of the ways we get witnesses to come here is to offer them protection. And if the first witness who gets protection ends up going back to Bosnia with his name in the newspaper, this case is in jeopardy, and that's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a serious allegation to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I don't know if it's true. I don't know if it's true, but it occurred to me, and as I was watching that cross-examination, I did not see any relationship or need to bring up that person's name in the way that he did, because it was clear this witness had left Ahmici in October of '92, and the other witness did not get into Ahmici until February of '93, and that was clear. I don't know if the allegation is true, but I can tell you that I am not very happy about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I know. But let us assume it was a slip of the tongue, and let us make sure that this will not be repeated. I mean, this will not happen again. I think Judge May made an excellent suggestion, namely, that you should get in touch with Defence counsel and discuss this matter thoroughly. I understand that probably the parties are keen to know what we are going to do next week, whether we are going to have hearings -- yes, as scheduled, we will have hearings the whole of next week, except for Friday afternoon, which will be off, as usual, and then also the third week starting on the 31st of August. Then only on Monday, the 31st of August, on Monday afternoon, Monday afternoon will be off, and Friday afternoon, the 4th of September will also be off. Otherwise, we will go on. Then we will let you know about further plans. We don't know yet. We will probably know next week whether we are going to be busy with another trial, depending on the decision by members of the Appeals Chamber. Therefore, we are not in a position to tell you whether we can sit for four or five weeks in a row. It is sure that we are going to sit for three weeks in a row until the 4th of September, in any case, but probably we will also need for the Prosecution case two more weeks. What is your guess, Mr. Moskowitz? Judging from the pace of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, probably we will need not the three weeks, which had been envisaged by the Prosecution, but at least five weeks only for the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would think at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: At least, so five to six weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you don't mind, by the end of next week, we will let you know whether we will continue after the three full weeks with two or three more weeks, or whether we will have a recess of one week. As I say, it depends on another case. If there are no further matters, I will suggest that we rise now. We will reconvene on Monday morning at 9.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 12.08 a.m. to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of August, 1998 at 9.30 a.m.
